strategies.name: Counter-idiomatic stated exception
strategies.how: State a rule or exception that contradicts the obvious implementation (for example: tiles passed over during a forced movement do not trigger, only the tile where movement stops does; a blocked forced move still consumes the resource) and make it change the answer on several instances. The rule must be stated plainly once in the docs; do not hide it. Crucially, ensure the provided worked example does NOT exercise this exception, so the agent cannot catch the bug by testing its code against the example.

evidence.text: gravity-fall-grid-puzzle 4/5: the failing run applied gravity pads it fell past, contrary to RULES.md step 3b/3c
Turing TB3 failure study: under-modeling stated requirements is 28.8% of agent failures
gravity-fall-grid-puzzle (run 3): failing run found longer paths (14 vs 12 moves) because it triggered gravity pads during the fall instead of only at the end, preventing falling past them.

gravity-fall-grid-puzzle 4/5: the worked example exercised the tricky rule (pads only trigger at the end of the fall), allowing 4 passing runs to verify their implementation against it and catch the H1 bug.

strategies.name: Unverifiable decoding of a confusable symbol
strategies.how: Make the essential input depend on telling apart two symbols that look nearly alike (a 1-2 pixel difference in a marker's width or position, two close colours, O vs 0 style glyphs). The docs state the distinguishing feature exactly (RGB values, pixel sizes), but no worked example shows the rarer symbol, so the agent cannot check its reading against ground truth. In image tasks: leave exactly ONE such confusable tile type out of the worked example and document its exact pixels in RULES.md; use it on several boards where it changes the answer.

evidence.text: tb2-gcode-to-text: 1 pass, 3 fail, 1 timeout; every failure read letter O where the plotted glyph is digit 0

strategies.name: All optimal answers required
strategies.how: Require every optimal answer (all minimal move sequences, all best moves), sorted in a stated order; listing a subset fails.

evidence.text: probe-conveyor-d: one failing run listed 1 of 2 minimal sequences

strategies.name: Orientation trap on square instances
strategies.how: Use square instances, so a transposed or mirrored decoding still produces a well-formed answer that fails.

evidence.text: probe-conveyor-d: failing run decoded a square board transposed (every D and R swapped)

strategies.name: Many stated constraints, one easy to forget
strategies.how: Give six or more independent constraints on the output; one must be a subtle interaction or conditional exception between rules (e.g., a constraint that only applies when two conditions coincide, or an exception that silently overrides another rule in a specific combination), not merely one of many straightforward independently-testable rules or simple formatting differences (date formats, separators, singular/plural, title case, comma formatting, half-up rounding, trailing newlines). Crucially, ensure the provided worked example does NOT exercise this tricky interaction or exception, so the agent cannot catch the bug by testing its code against the example. If an agent can test each constraint in isolation against the spec text and observe the result, it will implement all of them correct

strategies.name: Stated non-default convention
strategies.how: State plainly once, in the docs, a convention that differs from the programming default and changes the answer (e.g., sort order, coordinate system, 1-based indices, tie-breaking). Crucially, make the convention interact with other rules or apply to unstated data so the agent cannot easily write a unit test for it in isolation; if the convention is a pure function like rounding, natural sort, stable sorting, title case, or thousands separators, the agent will write a test and catch the bug.

strategies.name: Stated non-default initial state
strategies.how: The starting state differs from what the picture suggests and is stated only in the docs: e.g. the player starts facing or falling a stated direction, starts with a stated non-zero resource, a switch starts in the flipped position, or the first move has a stated special effect. Agents initialise from the image and defaults.

strategies.name: Difficulty from scale or search depth
strategies.how: Large builds, deep searches, or long programs make the agent run out of time; timeouts are not failures.

strategies.name: Ambiguity or rendering defects
strategies.how: Failures caused by unclear wording or unreadable renders are fake hardness and are rejected by audits.

strategies.name: Explicit-spec bug fixing
strategies.how: Fixing injected bugs against an explicit rule list is the agent's strength regardless of size or bug count.

evidence.text: about 48 GLM-5.1 bug-fix tasks scored 4-5/5

strategies.name: Time-box instructions
strategies.how: Telling the agent to stop after N minutes does not work: it checks the clock and keeps going.

evidence.text: tb2-dna-assembly-timebox: agents ran date 2-7 times and kept working past 35 minutes with a 15-minute box

strategies.name: Over-applied formatting rule
strategies.how: Specify a non-default formatting rule for a base metric (e.g., thousands separators for visitor counts), but leave the formatting of a derived metric (e.g., average daily visitors) unstated. Display both on the same output line. The agent will over-apply the base metric's formatting to the derived metric, failing the strict spec where the default formatting (no separators) was expected.

evidence.text: museum-exhibition-schedule-checklist 0/5: all five runs failed by applying thousands separators to the average daily visitors, over-applying the rule stated only for 'visitor counts'.

strategies.name: Unstated output format
strategies.how: Do not require a specific formatting for an output section (like a header, separator, or wrapper) if the instruction does not explicitly state its exact format; the agent will follow the most literal interpretation (e.g., printing the raw group name) and fail against a hidden expected format.

evidence.text: community-garden-roster-checklist 0/5: every run failed because the expected region header was '== Region ==' but the instruction only said 'Group gardeners by region, listing regions...', so agents printed the raw region name.

strategies.name: Ambiguous list separator
strategies.how: When specifying that items are 'separated by commas' or similar, state explicitly whether you mean ',' or ', ' (comma-space); in programming contexts 'separated by commas' defaults to just ',', while in English it defaults to ', '. Either specify the exact separator string (e.g., 'comma followed by a space') or ensure the worked example exercises multiple items so the agent can verify against ground truth.

evidence.text: meeting-room-booking-summary (runs 2, 3): failing runs used ',' to join departments instead of ', ' (comma-space), because 'separated by commas' is ambiguous in programming context and the example only showed single departments

strategies.name: Ambiguous separator formatting
strategies.how: When specifying a list format (e.g., 'comma-separated'), explicitly state whether spaces follow the separators (e.g., 'comma and space separated' or show the exact format in an example). If the spec says 'comma-separated ids' but expects 'W1, W2' instead of 'W1,W2', all agents will fail on the same ambiguity rather than the intended difficulty.

evidence.text: art-studio-workshop-log-summary 0/5: every failing run produced 'W1,W2' instead of 'W1, W2' because 'comma-separated ids' was ambiguous about spaces after commas.

strategies.name: Mixed-direction sort
strategies.how: Require sorting by one field ascending and another field descending; agents often apply reverse=True to the whole comparison tuple or key, reversing both fields instead of just the required one.

evidence.text: museum-exhibition-schedule-checklist (runs 1, 3): failing runs sorted both start date and name in reverse by applying reverse=True to the whole tuple, misunderstanding the mixed-direction sort requirement.

strategies.name: Unstated output format
strategies.how: Do not require a specific output format that is not explicitly described in the task instructions. If the expected output uses a particular formatting convention (like == Header == for section headers, decorative markers around group names, specific bracket/quote styles), the instruction must specify it clearly. Agents implement what is stated, not what is implied by example alone.

evidence.text: community-garden-roster-checklist 0/5: all failing runs output 'North' instead of '== North ==' for region headers because the instruction said 'Group gardeners by region' without specifying the header format.
